Run a script on the real data

real_run.Rd

Runs the researcher's script on the real data in a fresh, isolated R session inside the secure environment. Output is kept in output_dir, and a log of the code (optionally with its printed output, cleaned of data values) is placed next to the output. Check the output with inspect() before anything is released.

Usage

real_run(
  script,
  real_data,
  output_dir,
  timeout = 3600,
  config = NULL,
  raw_log = NULL,
  log = c("code_only", "cleaned")
)

Arguments

script

Path to an R script, or R code as text.

real_data

The real data: a data frame (available to the script as data) or a named list of data frames (available under their names).

output_dir

Directory for the output. Created if needed; must be empty, so only output from this run can be released.

timeout

Maximum run time in seconds.

config

A mimic_config(); NULL uses the defaults. The script's safe_count(), safe_summary() and safe_model() follow it.

raw_log

Optional path where the uncleaned log is saved for staff. It must lie outside output_dir and must not be released.

log

"code_only" (the default) keeps only the code; "cleaned" also keeps its printed output with data values removed. See What the log contains.

Value

An object of class mimic_run that is safe to pass on to the researcher: status ("ok" or "error"), error (the safe error report, see below), files written, blocked writes, log_file (the cleaned log in output_dir), redactions and warnings (cleaned).

Safe error report

When the script fails, the researcher cannot see the data to find out why. real_run() returns what helps without revealing anything:

  • the error class and the function that raised it,

  • the line in the script,

  • the error message with data values removed: quoted parts that are not words from the script or names in the data become <value>, every number becomes <n>, and identifiers, free text and rare values are removed,

  • for every variable mentioned in the script or the message: class, share missing (rounded), number of distinct values, whether there are empty strings, and whether it is entirely missing.

The full call is never kept, because a call can carry a whole data frame.

What the log contains

The script is run with source(echo = TRUE). By default (log = "code_only") the log keeps only the code, and each stretch of printed output becomes <output not kept>. The researcher sees where the script got to, but no output; results must come as files that inspect() checks.

With log = "cleaned" the printed output is kept too, with values that could point to a person replaced by <value>: identifiers, free text, and any value (string, date or number with at least three digits, or a rare age or other small number in a quasi-identifier) held by fewer than min_count persons. Persons are counted on the identifier columns of each table, so a code one person has on many contacts is still rare. Numbers are compared at the precision they are printed with, so the minimum shown by summary() as 38390 is found even when the value is 38389.6, and also when written with thousands separators (9.800.000, 38,390). Dates are found in the common ways of writing them (1959-01-31, 31.01.1959, 31/01/1959, 31011959), and free text also when only its first part is printed. A line with two or more such values is removed entirely: it is most likely a printed row, and the common values left in it (sex, settlement, occupation) could still single out a person in a small place. Common values elsewhere are left, so the log stays readable.

Cleaning is a search for known values, so it cannot find what a script has transformed: a name in capitals, a date with the month spelled out, a piece cut from the middle of a note, a value divided by 1000. A line with a single rare value also keeps its common values, and those can still be a rare combination when a script prints rows. That is why the code-only log is the default; choose the cleaned log for scripts staff have read.

The names of files the script wrote, and of writes that were blocked, are cleaned the same way, because a script can name a file after a person.

real_run() does not know the keys of the tables. Persons are found through identifier columns: names like person_id, id, cpr... or pnr..., and the id_vars of the configuration. When the key has another name (lbnr, person), add it to id_vars; otherwise rare values are counted in rows, and a code one person has on twelve contacts looks common.

Limits

Write calls in base R, utils, grDevices and common packages (data.table, readr, writexl, openxlsx, haven, arrow, ggplot2, qs, fst, ...) are blocked when they target a path outside output_dir. This is a safety net, not a sandbox: a determined script can write elsewhere through other functions. File system permissions in the secure environment must enforce what may be written where.

The data are passed to the child session through a temporary file that callr deletes afterwards; it lies in the session's temporary directory inside the secure environment.

Examples

# \donttest{
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "run1")
r <- real_run(c(
  "tab <- table(persons$sex)",
  "write.csv(as.data.frame(tab), 'sex.csv', row.names = FALSE)"
), list(persons = fake_persons), out)
r
#> <mimic_run> (code)
#> ✔ The script ran through on the real data in under a second.
#> ℹ Output files: sex.csv
#> ℹ Check the output with `inspect()` before release.

# a failing script gets a safe error report
r2 <- real_run("fit <- lm(income ~ settlment, data = persons)",
               list(persons = fake_persons), file.path(tempdir(), "run2"))
r2
#> <mimic_run> (code)
#> ✖ The script failed at line 1.
#> Message (data values removed): object 'settlment' not found
#> Variables involved:
#>    table variable   class missing    distinct empty_strings all_missing
#>  persons   income numeric     3 % about 1,615            NA       FALSE
#> ℹ No output files.
#> ℹ Check the output with `inspect()` before release.
# }
